newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Legislators back Cape Town Olympic bid.
newsitem.headline: Legislators back Cape Town Olympic bid.

text.p: The multi-party sports and recreation committee of South Africa's parliament on Tuesday pledged support for Cape Town's bid to host the 2004 Olympic Games.
Cape Town is rated with Rome and Stockholm as front runners in the 11-city race to host the games and would be the first African city to stage the event.

Former banker Chris Ball, chief executive of the non-profit bid company managing the project, briefed members of parliament on proposals contained in the formal "Bid Book" presented to the International Olympic Committee last month.

Several legislators spoke in promised support for the bid and African National Congress veteran Ellen Kuzwayo wrapped up with an emotional endorsement of the project, adding: "We must get the Games, by hook or by crook."
She said opponents of the project should be "thrown into the sea."
Stressing the developmental potential of the Games for Cape Town, South Africa and the continent, Ball said:
"If one brings the Olympic Games to Africa there would be a dramatic impact in terms of economic growth and human development.
"There would be a world focus on Africa in terms of sport and cooperation, rather than famine and war."
Ball said the bid was based on guaranteed revenue of $1.3 billion at 1996 prices, of which two-thirds would go to operating costs.

Calculations backed by the Southern African Development Bank indicated a 30 billion rand ($6.67 billion) boost to South Africa's gross domestic product by the end of the games and a further five billion rand every year thereafter.
He said the conservative estimate was for 100,000 permanent jobs as a result of the games.
"The returns are very high and the risk is very modest. This is a solid, sound and conservative development plan for the Western Cape," he said.

Ball said work would be under way by November, when the IOC evaluation team arrives to assess the city, on five Olympic venues and one more would be built in each of the seven remaining years if Cape Town wins the bid.
He listed crime, transport and accommodation as the major challenges facing Cape Town's bid.
